A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, despite the changed title and publication format. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on generated and spoofed text, including false-positive rates, detection power, model comparisons, and validation analyses in Sections 5 and Appendices A–C.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds experiments on reference-corpus mismatch, attacker training size, reprompting alternatives, additional watermark schemes, and modified watermarked text.

M1.justification: Section 4.2 and Appendix G extend the detector beyond binary Red-Green colors. AAR uses negative-log watermark scores; KTH introduces Levenshtein alignment costs and a surrogate context of h = 5. These are substantive scheme-specific scoring adaptations, while the original Standard and Reprompting procedures remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds Wikipedia, Repliqa, and Math as reference corpora and OpenWebText for fixed-corpus calibration. It also evaluates new input scenarios involving AAR/KTH watermarks, insertion of human text, and DIPPER paraphrasing (Appendices D, F–H). C4 and Dolly coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Appendix F.2 newly evaluates a fixed-corpus correlation estimator as an alternative to Reprompting. The principal evaluated spoofing methods remain Stealing and Distillation; extending Distillation evaluation to AAR/KTH does not introduce another attack comparator.

E3.justification: The original Section 5 setup is retained, but substantial new protocols are added: LLAMA3-8B/QWEN2.5-7B model configurations, attacker training-size sweeps, perturbed reference counts, fixed-corpus calibration, and AAR/KTH settings. Edited-text experiments specify insertion proportions and separate sample counts for mixing and paraphrasing (Appendices A.5, D–H).

E4.justification: New analyses test sensitivity to reference-corpus mismatch and attacker training size, the effect of estimating prompts, and the necessity of reprompting versus fixed calibration. Additional robustness experiments examine another model pair and false positives after text insertion or paraphrasing. The original concatenation and context-dependence analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Section 5.1 and Figure 2 supplement v1's visual normality assessment with Kolmogorov–Smirnov and Pearson normality tests, reporting p-values and rejection decisions. Figure 9 adds distributional boxplots with explicitly defined whiskers. Neither version reports repeated-seed uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in v1 Tables 1–5 are retained in v2 Tables 1, 5, 2, 3, and 4, respectively. Substantial new results appear in Figures 6 and 9–15. For example, Appendix G reports about 90% AAR detection with 500 tokens at nominal 1% rejection, accompanied by approximately 2% empirical false positives. These results concern newly evaluated conditions.

T1.justification: v2 adds a general mathematical representation of watermark transformations and nonbinary score definitions for AAR/KTH. Lemma 4.1, its assumptions, and its proof remain unchanged, moving from Appendix D to Appendix I. No corresponding generalized proof accompanies the new extensions.

C1.justification: v1 frames its contributions around Red-Green watermark schemes; v2's introduction additionally claims generalization to all schemes vulnerable to learning-based spoofing, with AAR/KTH demonstrations. The abstract and conclusion also explicitly qualify the previously broader 'all current spoofing methods' language as learning-based attacks.

C2.justification: Appendices D–F add substantive interpretations of reference-data mismatch, attacker data scaling, and why reprompting is preferable to fixed calibration. v2 also acknowledges AAR false-positive inflation, explicitly identifies short input length as a limitation, and expands discussion of edited text, piggyback spoofing, and watermark security trade-offs.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link and specifies previously unstated attacker training-data sizes: 30,000 samples of 800 tokens for Stealing and 640,000 samples of 256 tokens for Distillation. New appendices document additional experimental parameters. The training-size disclosures do not establish changes to the retained experiments.

R1.justification: Sections 2 and Appendix J substantially expand research positioning around learning-based, piggyback, and step-by-step spoofing, deployed watermarks, and cryptographic defenses. New citations include Aaronson, Dathathri et al., Christ and Gunn, and recent watermark-identification work. Existing publication-year and venue updates are separate from these substantive additions.

P1.justification: v2 changes the title, rewrites substantial introductory material, combines background and related work in Section 2, and moves the spoofer-model study from Section 5.3 to Appendix A.4. The appendices are extensively reorganized, and impact and acknowledgment sections replace the earlier document's closing structure.

P2.justification: The main paper changes to a two-column layout with resized and relocated displays. The spoofer-model table and figure move to Appendix A, eight new figures are added, and Figure 2 gains p-values and colored normality-test indicators. The five original tables remain, with renumbering and layout adjustments.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens practical validation by testing assumptions that v1 left largely unchecked: reference-corpus mismatch, prompt estimation, fixed calibration, and modifications to genuine text. These experiments clarify when the detector works and expose a failing calibration alternative; added code-access information also helps reproducibility. The broader generalization claim remains limited by AAR false-positive inflation and the absence of an extended proof, but these qualifications do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and applicability assessment.
